stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Archaeologists compared wooden tools buried in two kinds of soil at the same site. Tools in dry, sandy soil, where air moves freely, had mostly rotted away. Tools in waterlogged clay, which holds very little oxygen, were nearly intact. The team concluded that oxygen is what drives the decay. Based on this finding, draining the clay so that air could reach it would likely ______
choices: slow the decay of the tools buried in the clay.
speed the decay of the tools buried in the clay.
speed the decay of the tools buried in the sand.
speed the decay of every tool buried at the site.
explanation: Write the finding as one arrow: more oxygen → faster decay. Clay tools survived because the clay held little oxygen. Draining the clay lets air in, so oxygen goes up for the clay tools, and their decay should speed up. Both the direction (speed) and the group (clay) have to be right. This is the basic move behind every 'apply the finding to a new case' inference question: write the arrow first, then push the change through it.

A.why: You picked the right group but flipped the direction. Draining adds oxygen, and the passage says oxygen drives decay, so decay speeds up. It does not slow down.

C.why: This is the swapped-group trap. The direction is right, but the change happens to the clay. The sandy soil already had air, and draining the clay does nothing to it.

D.why: You stretched one group's change to everything. Draining the clay changes conditions only in the clay. The sand tools' situation stays the same.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: A city planning office tracked summer pavement temperatures after planting street trees. On low-rise residential blocks, the new trees lowered pavement temperatures noticeably. On downtown blocks lined with tall buildings, which already cast heavy shade, the trees made no measurable difference. If the city later removed the street trees, the study suggests that pavement temperatures would likely ______
choices: rise on downtown blocks but not on residential blocks.
fall on residential blocks but not on downtown blocks.
rise on residential blocks but not on downtown blocks.
rise on both residential blocks and downtown blocks.
explanation: The arrow is: trees → cooler pavement, but only on residential blocks. Removing the trees runs that arrow backward, so pavement gets warmer on residential blocks. Downtown blocks never changed when trees were added, so removing the trees shouldn't change them either. This is the split-result version of the question type: one group responds and one doesn't, and the answer has to keep that split.

A.why: This is the swapped-group trap. The direction is right, but the trees only ever affected residential blocks. Downtown blocks showed no difference.

B.why: You picked the right group but flipped the direction. The trees cooled the pavement, so taking them away makes it warmer, not cooler.

D.why: You ignored half of the finding. The study says trees made no measurable difference downtown, so you have no grounds to predict a change there.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Cartographers often assume that shaded relief, the soft shadowing that makes hills look raised, helps everyone read a map. A recent study complicates that view. Shading improved how accurately first-time hikers judged which slopes were steepest, but experienced hikers judged slopes equally well with or without it. If shading were left off a trail map, the study suggests that slope judgments would likely ______
choices: become less accurate for first-time hikers only.
become more accurate for first-time hikers only.
become less accurate for experienced hikers only.
become less accurate for all hikers alike.
explanation: The arrow is: shading → better accuracy, for first-time hikers only. Take the shading away and their accuracy drops. Experienced hikers did equally well with or without it, so they shouldn't be affected. The passage also corrects a popular view ('helps everyone'), so the answer has to follow the corrected version, not the original assumption.

B.why: You picked the right group but flipped the direction. Shading helped first-time hikers, so removing it hurts their accuracy. It doesn't improve it.

C.why: This is the swapped-group trap. Experienced hikers did equally well with or without shading. Only first-time hikers depended on it.

D.why: You went back to the popular view the passage corrects. The study shows shading mattered for only one group, so you can't predict a loss for everyone.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many schools hang handwashing posters wherever students are most likely to see them. A study of school cafeterias, however, found that location matters. Posters hung directly beside the sinks increased handwashing before lunch, while identical posters hung at the cafeteria entrance, away from the sinks, had no effect. The study suggests that a school moving its posters from the sinks to the entrance would ______
choices: increase handwashing, since only entrance posters raised it.
increase handwashing, since only sink posters raised it.
stop handwashing, since only sink posters raised it.
reduce handwashing, since only sink posters raised it.
explanation: The arrow is: poster beside the sink → more handwashing. A poster at the entrance has no effect. Moving the posters takes away the version that worked and puts up one that does nothing, so handwashing should fall back down. Both halves of the answer have to be right: the direction (reduce) and the group (the sink posters were the ones that worked).

A.why: This is the swapped-group trap. You gave the effect to the wrong location. The passage says the entrance posters had no effect.

B.why: You picked the right location but the wrong direction. If only the sink posters raised handwashing, removing them lowers it.

C.why: This is strength creep. Students washed their hands before any posters went up. Losing the boost brings handwashing down, not to zero.
